en: Shi Dunlun’s Collected Exegesis on the Treatise, Fascicle Eighty-Two.
Of the seven sections above, the first four have already been explained. Now, the fifth—Establishing Others—is being explained.
Listen. This constitutes the first [section], which explains the essence of the teaching;
the second [section] distinguishes the method of interpretation.
Having thus established the virtues of the Dharma-preacher endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge,
next we shall clarify how he teaches the various dharmas while situated among the fivefold assembly.
Since he is teaching the Dharma within the assembly:
Settle the people so that they abide in reverence and listen without error;
first increasing from one to ten,
this clarifies the causes for listening.
Regarding the four permutations— such as "beneficial but not pleasant" and so forth— as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
that which is beneficial but not pleasant is,
for example, the practice of asceticism and the observance of precepts in the present life.
Tranquility is not what is truly beneficial.
What is currently experienced as defiled pleasure is termed "tranquil happiness," yet its essence is not wholesome.
That which does not bring about benefit in future lives is not beneficial.
That which possesses both [benefit and happiness] refers to the practice of wholesome states (*kuśala*) associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
Regarding "neither":
it refers to performing acts such as killing that are associated with painful feelings.
Regarding the "two causes": [they are]...
First, the Dharma is well-established; second, it possesses superior fruits.
That which can swiftly be realized and understood as vast and profound is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
That which is "similarly profound" refers to the two kinds of emptiness.
These two kinds of emptiness are the gate for realizing true suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, they are called "similar.
As for all dependently originated phenomena,
they are suchness and the two emptinesses.
All are manifested through the principle of dependent origination;
thus the treatise says: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty.
One who is able to sever the five dharmas and cultivate the seven dharmas [attains this realization].
It is the severing of the five hindrances and the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Regarding the statement that "all phenomena of origination are phenomena of cessation":
afflictions, karma, and so forth are termed phenomena of origination.
By means of hearing the Dharma, all [faults] are eliminated.
Within the seventh section, the sixth part explains the brief and extensive praise of the Buddha.
In this, first, the general outline establishes the topical headings.
Second, the detailed explanation. This consists of a brief exposition followed by an extensive one.
Within the brief exposition, there are two parts.
First, the praise of the Buddha is elucidated by means of five aspects;
subsequently, it is elucidated by means of six aspects.
Regarding "being free from defilement":

"Free from entanglements and stains" means being free from the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). "Without turbidity or impurity" means being free from the latent dispositions (*anusaya*).
Furthermore, regarding the initial abandonment of afflictions and the subsequent abandonment of karma,
there are fourteen sections in brief and detailed praise.
The first is the praise of the six virtues.
Second, praising the four virtues;
third, praising the five virtues;
fourth, praising the six virtues.
5. Praising the seven virtues;
6. Praising the eight virtues;
7. Praising the eight virtues.
The so-called "threefold tranquility" refers to the tranquility of body, speech, and mind.
[This concludes] the eight praises and ten titles.
Ninth, praising the twenty-two virtues;
tenth, praising the five virtues in both general and specific terms—
namely, that "Arhat" is the general term.
The four wisdoms are distinct.
The eleven [verses] praise the six virtues.
Regarding this, Master Jing said:
"Permanently severing the five factors" means severing the five higher fetters (*pañca-ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
"Accomplishing the six factors" means:
These constitute the six ever-present factors (*sad-anuvartaka-dharmāḥ*), because mindfulness, wisdom, and equanimity constantly arise within the gates of the six consciousnesses.
Master Ki says:
"Severing the five branches" means severing the five higher fetters as well as the five lower fetters.
"Accomplishing the six branches" means:
One accomplishes the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
Furthermore, one accomplishes the six factors of practice (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) as previously explained in the thirty-fourth fascicle.
Now, according to the Āgama Sūtras, it is said that the fruit of arhatship crushes the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇa),
guards the six abodes (ṣaḍ-āvāsa),
and attains mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati).
He subdues the four māras and so forth.
Thus, within this context, his six virtues are praised:
first, he has severed the five hindrances.
Second, one accomplishes the six constant abodes;
third, one attains the four foundations of mindfulness;
fourth, one subdues the four māras.
5. The Purely Wholesome Accumulation;
6. The Supreme Person; 12.
Praise of the Seven Dharmas; 13. Praise of the Nine Virtues.
Fourteen verses praise eight virtues.
The preceding section has been a praise of virtues;
alternatively, this may be a detailed expansion upon the brief praise of virtues mentioned above.
There may be other praises of virtues not mentioned in the brief summary,
which can be understood by consulting the text.
Among the seven sections, the seventh explains the benefits of training (*śikṣānuśaṃsa*).
Regarding the Chinese text, there are two parts:
first, an explanation based on the essence, clarifying how he preached the Dharma in five sections for the great assembly;
second, a sequential explanation of the scriptural passages concerning the benefits of training.
Regarding what was previously stated— that when various Dharma-preachers arrive at either the words or the meaning—
one should first investigate the six aspects within the words and the ten aspects within the meaning.
To cause them to attain thorough mastery means to penetrate the essential nature of the aforementioned phenomena;
subsequently, it extends even to the proclamation of the True Dharma.
In the section on the exegesis of the text, the difficulty regarding the meaning of the arising of dharmas is followed by five kinds of explanations of the underlying principle;
therefore, this is called the "fivefold explanation for the sake of others.
This cites the preceding essence and the explanation together as one.
Furthermore, one should likewise establish oneself as having attained the ten kinds of perfection;
this is the second [section] clarifying the qualities of the teacher.
As it was said in the previous fascicle:
"The teacher" refers to one who has accomplished the ten dharmas, and so forth, as explained at length.
Having thus established himself, he is established as one who teaches the Dharma to the assembly.
Next, the third [topic], the assembly for teaching, is clarified.
Furthermore, one should establish others so that they remain respectful and listen without error;
this is the fourth [requirement] regarding the audience.
Moreover, one should first praise the virtues of the Great Master.
This is the fifth summary of the praise of virtues.

Thus, one who expounds the True Dharma in these five parts generates joy for both oneself and others—just like a five-part musical performance—and is further able to bring about the benefit of both oneself and others.
This is the sixth clarification regarding the benefits of training.
At the beginning of the previous fascicle, the third verse was explained in six parts;
it is based on the text in this section that this determination is made.
Regarding the statement that if one can thus train well, one should know that five kinds of benefits are fully possessed:
this means that within each of the five preceding sections, all five benefits are present.
Furthermore, one may obtain five kinds of benefits through the fivefold analysis:
first, because one penetrates the essential meaning of the explanations,
it is not difficult to understand the words and meanings of the Buddha’s teachings.
Second, by virtue of the teacher’s qualities being able to perfectly fulfill the explanation of the characteristics of all phenomena;
third, by virtue of teaching the Dharma within an assembly,
being able to effectively arouse vast joy in both oneself and others.
Fourth, because it enables the assembly to listen with composure,
it can lead them toward virtue and liberation,
such that praise and renown pervade among both gods and humans.
Fifth, by praising the Buddha both briefly and extensively,
one can generate immeasurable merit.
From this point downward, the second section provides a detailed explanation by enumerating the benefits of training.
In the sutra there are four statements.
First: "You bhikṣus should dwell securely and train yourselves in the benefits.
This is the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā).
Second, wisdom is the foremost;
third, liberation is firm;
fourth, mindfulness is predominant.
Regarding these four propositions,
the text provides a detailed explanation through two sequential methods of exposition.
First is the method based on their essential nature (*tattva*).
Next, regarding the Śramaṇa tradition:
within the preceding section, there is first the general and then the specific.
Furthermore, as stated in the sūtra, one should know that the essence of this sūtra’s words and meaning consists in abiding in the benefits of training (*śikṣānuśaṃsa*).
This passage provides a general overview.
What follows is a detailed analysis,
first of the text and then of its meaning.
Regarding the term "words and letters":

this refers to the statement in this sutra, "O bhikṣus, you should dwell securely and train yourselves in the superior benefits," which clarifies the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) and the others.
Regarding the statement that there are twelve characters here: you [monks] have twelve characters in your name.
As for "four names constitute one sentence":
the phrase "you, bhikṣus" constitutes one name.
"Abiding" is the second name;
"training" is the third name, which refers to the three trainings (triśikṣā);
and "victory" is the fourth name.
Although the four names are distinct,
they equally clarify the single training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*), which is called "one phrase.
In this way, it encompasses the bodies of phrases, sentences, and syllables.

When that sutra text explains these twelve characters of the training in ethics (*śīla-śikṣā*) as four names (*nāman*) and one phrase (*pada*), it subsumes the first three among the six categories of the text:
name-body (*nāma-kāya*), phrase-body (*pada-kāya*), and syllable-body (*vyañjana-kāya*).
Regarding the statement that "the verbal expression herein, which constitutes the characteristics of the training (śikṣāpada), subsumes the characteristics of practice":
the names, phrases, and syllables associated with this verbal expression therein are the objects of training;
they are the mental characteristics that should be attended to.
This immediately subsumes the aspect of the practice.
To say that the Tathāgata’s discourse was fundamentally for the sake of the bhikṣus’ inquiries subsumes the "capable ones" who request it;
for that sūtra already states, "You bhikṣus, etc."
As for "speech," this refers to the fact that these precepts were originally taught by the Buddha for the sake of bhikṣus;
thus, they constitute a response to a specific occasion.
The vocal sounds uttered by the Tathāgata are subsumed under the category of speech (*vāc*).
Therefore, it should be understood that a single phrase of this sutra encompasses all six textual passages.
Likewise, in such phrases as "wisdom is the foremost," one should understand each according to its respective correspondence.
As stated in that sutra, "wisdom is the foremost" comprises four characters;
it consists of one name and one phrase,
and also includes the aspects of practice, characteristics, invitation, and speech.
If it is said that liberation has firm mindfulness as its predominant factor, it likewise encompasses the six aspects;
this should be understood according to their respective correspondences.
Hereafter, the four lines of the sutra will be analyzed through various thematic gateways.
The meaning consists of ten sections.
Within this text, there are eight parts.
The first distinguishes [the stages] according to the *bhūmis*.
Regarding the statement that within the meaning of "ground" (*bhūmi*) only the *śrāvaka-bhūmi* is mentioned:

although seventeen grounds were previously distinguished, the reason why only the *śrāvaka-bhūmi* is mentioned here in the context of the meaning of "ground" is that the sutra says to the bhikṣus: [the passage from the scripture follows].
By clarifying this phrase, one knows it refers exclusively to the stage of the Śrāvaka;
alternatively, it may encompass all five stages.
If these four phrases are analyzed according to the five stages:
This comprises the five stages.
When the Sūtra speaks of "the excellence of training," it refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-bhūmi*);
this reiterates that the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) constitutes the stage of equipment.
"Wisdom as the foremost is the stage of application" means that wisdom functions through the sixteen aspects within the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth. "Liberation,
firmness, and mindfulness as predominant are the stage of seeing, the stage of cultivation, and the ultimate stage" means [the same].
Both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) sever the afflictions and attain liberation.
Regarding mindfulness: on the path of seeing there is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and on the path of cultivation there is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
In the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), the ten factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-aṅga*) likewise possess both mindfulness (*smṛti*) and liberation (*vimukti*) that are not lost.
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the stages.
Second, the analysis is conducted by way of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the excellence of training in the meaning of characteristics" and "the self-characteristics of ethical discipline (*śīla*)":
this clarifies that there are three kinds or five [categories] of the meaning of characteristics; first, the five beginning with "self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Next, there are five [categories] beginning with "different synonyms" (*paryāya*), and five beginning with "the referent" (*abhidheya*).

In this present passage, however, only the first category is treated by means of a fourfold alternative analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding specifically characterized (*svalakṣaṇa*) and generally characterized (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) phenomena.
Regarding the "excellence of training," this is the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Ethical discipline is a formative phenomenon (*rūpadharma*) and lacks association (*samprayoga*) or coexistence (*sahabhū*).
Therefore, it is merely the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding "wisdom being the foremost," this possesses two kinds of characteristics; that is to say, concerning the specific characteristic of wisdom, the essence of wisdom itself is the specific characteristic.
Regarding the statement that the basis, the companions, and the object are called "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):
the basis refers to the sense faculties;
the companions refer to the other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that arise simultaneously.
The object of focus is the objective field (*ālambana*).
Because its characteristics are collectively termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*), it is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the firmness of liberation": this refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of liberation.
Liberation is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Analytical cessation is the extinction of those afflictions; it is exclusively a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
When mindfulness is predominant, mindfulness itself is the specific characteristic.
Mindfulness is a mental factor associated with the mind,
and it likewise apprehends only its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Next, regarding the third stage of attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth:

Regarding the statement that "the excellence of training" does not refer to the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) themselves, but rather to the establishment of the locus for those mental orientations:
this clarifies that the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) is not the seven mental orientations,
but is solely the foundational locus upon which the mental orientations depend.
One should practice mental attention based upon the precepts.

Regarding "wisdom as the foremost," one should know that the mental attentions of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisamvedī*) and resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*) are exclusively the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
With wisdom as the foremost, the previous discussion regarding the stages within the grounds refers to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-bhūmi*), which is the distant portion.
Therefore, there are only two types of attention (*manasikāra*): that which discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) and that which is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*).
The "firmly established in liberation" indicates the mental attention up to the fruit.
According to the Abhidharma and other treatises, "detachment" refers to the abandonment of superior obstacles,
while "receptive joy" refers to the abandonment of intermediate obstacles.
The culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is the abandonment of the inferior grade of non-obstruction.
The mental attention to the fruit of the culmination of the preparatory application is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Now it is clarified that the firmness of liberation is the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is attained through the path of unimpeded liberation;
therefore, it is said to be "manifested.

The discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) is the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), while the attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsāmanasikāra*) is the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*).
Regarding that liberation, since it is firm and lacks functional capacity, it is not said to be manifest;
one should know that for those for whom mindfulness is predominant, this reveals the attention of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manasikāra*).
The essence of mindfulness merely recollects whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned;
because its objective referent is the same as that of the attention of investigation,
their common characteristics are made manifest.
According to this principle, regarding those things that should be established accordingly among the knowledges (*jñāna*) and so forth—
the benefits of training (*śikṣānuśaṃsa*) as explained by the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*)—
they should be established accordingly among the ten knowledges and so forth.
The term "and so forth" includes the six consciousnesses, the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), and the three gates of liberation.
Among the ten knowledges (*jñāna*):
Wisdom (prajñā) is the foremost, and in the future it will be equal to knowledge (jñāna),
because its stage is that of the preparatory ground (prayoga-bhūmi).
Alternatively, it serves as the predominant condition for liberation and mindfulness, yet it is not the ten knowledges.
Regarding the six consciousnesses:
the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) and liberation (*vimukti*) are not subsumed within the six consciousnesses;
the two types—wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*)—are associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
In contrast to the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*):
the thorough knowledge of firm liberation is one of the nine thorough knowledges;
whereas ethical discipline, wisdom, and mindfulness are not among the nine thorough knowledges.
The meaning of the three liberations may be understood by analogy.
The fourth line distinguishes them according to their bases (*āśraya*).
There are three such bases.
First, the basis of phenomena;
second, the basis of time;
third, the basis of the person (pudgala).
Furthermore, within the basis of the objective entity (*vastv-adhiṣṭhāna*), there are three types:
first, the basis of the fundamental objective entity;
second, the basis of the objective entity consisting in the attainment of skillful means.
Third, regarding the basis for the matter of compassion for others,
there are six fundamental matters and twelve matters concerning the attainment of skillful means.
There are five aspects regarding the matter of compassion for others,
as explained in the previous fascicle.
Now, concerning the meaning of the "basis" (*āśraya*), that which is subsumed under the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) pertaining to *nirvāṇa* is discussed.
Regarding the four phrases beginning with "the excellence of training" (*śikṣānuśaṃsa*), among the six fundamental matters, they refer exclusively to the sixth, which is *nirvāṇa*.
As for "pure conduct," among the twelve practices that constitute the means for attainment, these four phrases beginning with "the excellence of training" refer exclusively to pure conduct.

Regarding the basis for the act of compassion, among the five phrases, it is whichever of the latter three is appropriate—namely, instruction (*avavāda*), encouragement (*samādāpana*), and rejoicing (*anuśamsana*).
Therefore, it is said that one should give rise to instruction and so forth, up to rejoicing, as the occasion requires. "Instruction" refers to the giving of instruction, and so on, up to rejoicing.
Question: Regarding the four phrases beginning with "the excellence of training" (*śikṣā-viśeṣa*), why is "progressive advancement" (*viśeṣa-gati*) not mentioned among the fundamental matters?

Furthermore, among the twelve aspects of the skillful means for attainment, why are "separation," "virtuous conduct," "progressive advancement," "division of practice," and "practice for one's own benefit" not mentioned?
Among the five types of activities for benefiting others, why is the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*) and so forth not mentioned?
This is now explained:
it should be understood that within this context, there are also wholesome (*kuśala*) and other such practices.
According to what is most excellent, only the practice of purity is taught.

The preceding section, which sequentially traverses the three bases (*āśraya*) among the objects of study, concludes the fourfold textual passage concerning the benefits of training (*śikṣānuśaṃsa*) and so forth.
Hereafter, the fourfold scriptural passage concerning the benefits of training and so forth is presented in summary, in relation to the third base, the person (*pudgala*).
Previously, it was explained that there are twenty-seven bases for *pudgalas*.
Since the "advantages of training" apply only to those *pudgalas* who have gone forth,
it is said that the "one who has gone forth" (*pravrajita-pudgala*) is a basis for *pudgalas*.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that one should know Ānanda to be a "joyful one" (modaka) among all *pudgalas* of dull faculties and so forth:
within the twenty-seven types of persons, those who possess the status of being members of the ordained community (*pravrajita*) are complete in all four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among those who have gone forth, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties;
there are also seven types based on their practice;
and there are three types based on their vows.
It refers exclusively to śrāvakas and not to other noble ones;
it refers exclusively to those who are capable of being saved.
Furthermore, there are nine [types] based on their conduct.

As stated in the subsequent text, with the exception of householders and those who are incurably obstructed, all others—excluding those who are not bound—are human beings and not devas, and are thus subsumed within the four categories.
Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, Ānanda, you should know that for all *pudgalas* of dull faculties and so forth, [the fruit] is attained by depending on time and basis;
furthermore, Ānanda, one should rejoice regarding the past and present times."
Regarding "because they have already realized and because they are correctly realizing":
the bhikṣus and others, having already realized and correctly realized the three trainings and their fruits throughout the two periods of the past and present, should rejoice.
Regarding the statement that "in the present time there is manifestation, and in the future time there is instruction and encouragement":
in the present, there is manifestation.
Regarding the future, he will arise as a teacher for the bhikṣus.
This fifth point is explained in terms of its benefits.
Within the meaning of "benefits," it refers to the fact that by practicing the three trainings, one swiftly attains their fulfillment; this is the meaning of "benefit."
Regarding these ten points, the sixth is now presented as the fifth;
this is the general explanation.
"All" refers to the bhikṣus who swiftly attain perfection in the three trainings—this is the benefit.
What is meant by "victory"? To state it briefly:
it is to offer praise regarding that which is worthy of praise, whether it be a phenomenon (*dharma*) or a person.
The sixth [section] distinguishes [the topic] by way of faults and afflictions.
Regarding the meaning of "faults and afflictions," it states that those who have gone forth should not engage in improper conduct nor should they store up surplus wealth.
This [point], which logically belongs with the fifth, is now placed here as the sixth.
Regarding the meaning of those faults:
to state it briefly, it refers to the arising of revulsion toward either a phenomenon or a person that ought to be reviled and loathed.
The seventh [point] distinguishes this in terms of the objects to be remedied and their remedies.
There are two versions.
The second version states:
"Furthermore, all defiled activities are that which is to be remedied, while the practices of the three trainings and so forth are the remedies."
Regarding what is to be remedied,
in brief, it consists of all defiled activities.
As for the meaning of the remedy:
In brief, all pure practices can be understood by distinguishing them according to the eighth [category], both in their concise and extensive meanings.
The preceding section, based on the two gates of essence (*tattva*) and textual meaning (*artha*), has completed the analysis of the fourfold verse concerning the benefits of training and so forth.
From here on, the second section—based on the explanation according to the teaching—will analyze the fourfold scriptural text through five gates.
What is called the "difficult sequence of the meaning of the Dharma" constitutes the five reliances.
Because the first relies upon the Dharma, it is termed "study."
Because patience and precepts are purified, patience and the like are brought forth.
Furthermore, because one attains tranquility, one is called a "learner" (*śaikṣa*).
Through tranquility, one abandons immoral conduct and attains the coolness of ethical discipline.
Because it eliminates the defilements of karma,
it is called "training" (*śikṣā*).
As for the statement, "Furthermore, one should know [this] because of the characteristics previously explained, up to the causes and effects," it means:
To further explain the etymological definitions:
according to the gate of etymological definitions, there are five specific ways in which these names are explained.
From "precepts being named after their characteristics" up to "being named after cause and effect."
From "In the differentiation of the gates of meaning" onwards is the fourth section, the explanation of the differentiation of the gates of meaning.
Therein are five gates.
First, intrinsic nature;
second, realm;
third, time.
Regarding the four categories and five groups,
what is meant by "distinctions in intrinsic nature" refers to those ranging up to, or even exceeding, three hundred and fifty rules of training (śikṣāpada).
This clarifies that the sevenfold aggregate of śīla constitutes the essential nature of the precepts.
Within this, from the four pārājikas up to the seven methods for settling disputes, there are two hundred and fifty rules;
the remainder consists of the *saṃvara-śikṣāpada* (rules of training).
Taken as a whole, they constitute one category,
namely the *śaikṣa* precepts;
alternatively, they may be divided into two.
These are considered misdeeds and improper speech;
alternatively, they may be expanded into one hundred or even more categories.
Here, they are all included based on the great variety of modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Therefore, it is said that "it may exceed one hundred and fifty.
Regarding the distinction of realms— that which reaches up to what is not bound by a realm—
the Master Fan says:
The formless [attainments] are called meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
This designation applies both generally and specifically;
the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* employs it in its general sense.
Therefore, it also includes the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Just as the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) also extends to the formless realms,
if one relies on the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XIII), it says:
Regarding the morality of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the morality of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-śīla*),
the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are not called "meditative absorption.
The masters of the Abhidharma state that within the formless realm there is no maturation-form (*vipākaja-rūpa*).
Therefore, it is not mentioned in brief.
As for the establishment of the discipline of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-vinaya*),
it is because there is no coarse resultant form (*vipāka-rūpa*).
To speak precisely, this is the skillful means of emptiness;
it is also a remote counteragent,
for it remedies the violation of precepts regarding body and speech within the desire realm.
Regarding the volition associated with meditative concentration, one may also metaphorically establish the nature of the abstention from bodily and vocal acts;
the distinction of time can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the distinctions of stages:
although there are twenty-five distinctions of stages based on the preceding fascicle,
this present text discusses only five types through three gates.
To speak briefly, without discussing the five types and two categories:
those who have entered the True Dharma but are not yet accomplished are called "those of lower status.
Having entered the Buddha-dharma but not yet having achieved the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) is termed "lower status."
Furthermore, the stage of liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) may be designated as the lower level.
Next, there is a classification based on twenty-seven types of persons (pudgala).
First, regarding the two categories of lay and ordained, only the ordained are discussed; among them, there are four types.
First, citing sūtras of definitive meaning;
second, the thorough analysis of phenomena;
third, practice.
Fourth is the fruit.
Furthermore, practice is twofold:
first, wrong practice; [second, right practice].
Second, the fruit of right practice.
This also has two [aspects].
First, the fruit of wrong practice.
Second is the fruit of correct practice.
In this present sutra,

Regarding the statement that "it is called faith and compliance because it manifests as correct conformity toward all matters," this means that sentient beings apply diligence within their conviction regarding all matters taught by the Teacher, such as cause and effect.
Because faith arises by taking persons as its object,
it is called "opening faith. Because faith arises by taking phenomena as its object, [it is called "establishing faith"].

Regarding the statement "the holy life (brahmacarya) up to the practice of the dharma of sexual desire":
nirvana, being free from defilement, is called "holy" (brahma).

Furthermore, these eight branches arise from the Brahma-voice of that Tathāgata;

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) in terms of their stages: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five faculties and powers reside in the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*);
the seven factors of enlightenment reside in the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
The eightfold right path pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Although the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) possesses the seven factors of enlightenment,
it is only upon entering the path of seeing that one attains the ultimate by not arising from meditative concentration.
Therefore, the remaining six factors of enlightenment are collectively termed *śamatha* (calm abiding) within the context of the eightfold path of cultivation;
this is because the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant through its repeated investigation.
The remaining seven [factors] are collectively termed *vipaśyanā* (insight) because they arise from wisdom.

Among the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-sambhāra*), everything from the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the five powers (*pañca balāni*) is collectively termed "cultivating mindfulness of the body.
This differs from the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), which defines mindfulness of the body merely as the contemplation of the physical form (*rūpakāya*).
Regarding the statement, "Because they are of that nature and of that category as appropriate," etc.:
it is asked, since the seven factors of enlightenment in the path of vision (darśanamārga) are both determinate and indeterminate,

The commentary explains:
Among the factors of enlightenment in the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the factor of concentration (*samādhi*) is the essential nature (*svabhāva*);
the other six are its categories (*jāti*).
That which follows from these characteristics is called concentration (*samādhi*).
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) on the path of cultivation is its essential nature;
the remaining seven are its categories that follow from it, and thus they are called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Prior to the path of seeing, there are five factors:
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the five powers.
Among these, by mentioning the first and the last, they are termed "faith and wisdom."
These four foundations of mindfulness, according to the Mahāyāna, have mindfulness and wisdom as their essential nature;
therefore, among the first four foundations of mindfulness, only mindfulness is mentioned, while among the five powers, the power of faith is mentioned.
Both are common to concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
Therefore, it is said that within this context, faith and mindfulness are both common to these two categories.
By citing this, it is intended to clarify that the essence of the cultivation of mindfulness of the body is common to both concentration and wisdom.

The eighth [section], "Explaining [the Truths] as Being Like Illness and so forth," first provides a general heading.

The intent of the question is:
Why does the sutra describe [the aggregates] as being "like a disease" and so forth, yet does not explicitly state that they are "like a grave illness"?
In the response, first the general meaning is answered, followed by a specific explanation of the four practices.
Regarding the former: "Now, as for the practitioner reaching the observation of those fruits..."
This means that the practitioner first contemplates the Truth of Suffering by practicing the contemplation of impermanence;
next, they truly revile those phenomena as being like a disease and so forth, finding them utterly loathsome and repulsive;
and subsequently, they further contemplate impermanence, observing the fruit of suffering.
Because that practitioner contemplates impermanence at both the initial and final stages,
and contemplates illness during the intermediate stage,
the Sūtra says: "He regards them as like an illness, and so forth."
If one were to speak of them directly as being like a grave illness,
it would not be the same as contemplating their impermanence.
Next, the four modes of practice are explained individually.
First, the explanation of impermanence:

regarding the statement "that which is called impermanent extends to all things through successive transformation," this refers to observing the impermanence of a single body, which is termed the "contemplation of the physical body" (*janmakāya-vipaśyanā*).
Moment-to-moment impermanence is called a *kṣaṇa*.
Regarding the successive progression of *kṣaṇas*: because this or that contact arises and ceases, this or that sensation arises and ceases.

therefore, it is said that "this continuity sees.

two types are first set forth.
This will be explained separately later.
Within that, the first part explains the various sufferings such as birth.
Regarding the statement, "By seeing that the physical body arises through successive succession, one realizes and enters into the nature of suffering":
The arising and ceasing in every moment is called "suffering by nature," which is precisely the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Next, the three types of sensation are explained as all being suffering.
There are three successive expositions. The first states:
"Pleasurable sensations are suffering because they undergo transformation; all painful sensations are suffering because they arise and persist."
This text clearly states that when a painful sensation arises, it is painful while abiding;
therefore, it is "suffering-as-suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). It does not apply to unpleasant, pleasant, or neutral sensations.
The explanation of formations as perishing moment by moment:
because formations are accompanied by heaviness (*dausthulya*) and lack mastery, they are called "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
because their essence is impermanent and subject to destruction, they are said to be suffering.
The following is the second explanation.
That which has already perished is called suffering because of its impermanence;
this refers to the past.
That which has already arisen is also said to be suffering because it is of a nature to perish;
this refers to the present.
That which is of a nature to perish is likewise called suffering, and so forth.
The neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā) of the ālayavijñāna is of a nature subject to destruction;
at times it is accompanied by the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā),
and at times it is pursued by the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā).
Because it arises concomitantly with either of these two types of suffering,
it is called "associated"; thus,
this feeling of equanimity is also termed "suffering."
"From 'How should one contemplate it?
onwards is the third explanation;
that is to say, by means of this feeling, greed lies latent."
Because of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), one experiences suffering in the future;
and because in the present life they can give rise to conditions for the loss of pleasant feeling, which then produces distress, they constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
In this way, one should contemplate pleasant feeling as suffering.
How should one contemplate [feeling] as being like an arrow? Because it is constantly afflictive and destructive—this is the contemplation of painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
As for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and even the two types of painful and pleasant feelings: [the same applies].
In this contemplation, equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) are termed the two kinds of suffering and pleasure.

as they have already been discussed in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*. Regarding the eighth [topic],
the analysis of the elements (*dhātuvibhāga*), there are five types.
Regarding what is called the "element of cessation" (nirodha-dhātu):
it is named the element of cessation because the aggregate-body (skandha-kāya), which serves as the basis for the afflictions to be abandoned through vision and cultivation, has ceased.
The ninth [section] explains the two gradual sequences.
First, a general presentation;
second, a sequential explanation.
Within the section on the gradual sequence of the fruits of liberative knowledge,
the text is divided into two parts;
the first concerns four dharmas.
The latter is discussed in terms of the four attachments;
the tenth explains that [the self] is neither annihilated nor eternal.
The former is discussed in terms of the three periods of time.
Regarding the subsequent summary of the four conditions,
in the first [condition], because it takes non-abiding activity as its cause, it is the past.
Second, because there is no cause for abiding once [the dharma] has already arisen, it is the present.
Third, regarding the statement that "the causal nature of future conditioned phenomena ceases," this means that the impermanent dharmas of the present are the causes of the future.

The subsequent passage, which states that the "equal and immediate condition" (samanantarapratyaya) refers to the distinct six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors when they have ceased immediately prior,
explains that the five sensory consciousnesses serve as the equal and immediate condition for the [subsequent] five sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, there is continuity.
As for the statement in the first volume that the five consciousnesses lack an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
this is based on the "sudden-arising mind" (*saṃbhava-citta*).
If one relies on the principle of equal outflow (*niṣyanda*), it can also be continuous.
The eleventh [section] explains defilement and purity;
it first opens into two chapters.
Second, the explanation according to the topical outline.
This explanation has three parts;
first, the explanation of the three matters.
Next, the two characteristics are explained,
followed by a detailed analysis and re-explanation.
Regarding the concluding statement that summarizes the three matters into one name— namely, "arising through three matters" and so forth— the following is the explanation.
Although these three matters are distinct, they are collectively termed "observing defilement and purity.
Within the explanation of the two characteristics, it says:
"The first is by way of the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*)."
Because one contemplates the gratification, the disadvantage, and the nature of renunciation in that manner. Second,
by way of the nature of the full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*),
one contemplates all aspects of the gratification, the disadvantage, and the renunciation to the full extent of their existence.
It is said that herein, when one contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and perceives the arising of pleasure and the arising of joy, this is called "the gratification" (*āsvāda*).
Conditioned phenomena are that which is gratified.
Furthermore, this gratification is exceedingly slight.
Master Jing said:
It is called "narrow and small" because the occasions for generating joy and bliss within conditioned phenomena are few.
Master Tai said:
"Attachment to flavors is the cause; afflictions are called the fruit.
Because the characteristics of the fruit are manifold, it is termed 'vast'."
Because the fault is subtle, it is called "narrow and small.
Thus, by means of these two aspects, one contemplates the nature of things as they are (*yathābhūtatā*), namely, their gratifying flavor (*āsvāda*):
first, one contemplates that the practice gives rise to pleasure and joy.
Second, regarding the contemplation that the flavor of craving is extremely narrow while its faults are vast,
Master Jing says:
Because the meaning of "impermanence" extends to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*),
it is called "vast. As for the phrase "by means of two characteristics":
First, impermanence and so forth;
second, vastness.
Regarding the contemplation by way of two aspects within renunciation:
First, the emergence through the cessation and abandonment of sensual desire;
second, [the emergence] as tranquility, the unsurpassed, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the relish, the disadvantage, and the escape from all conditioned phenomena," and so on:
This is a general overview.
Furthermore, from "in order to understand" below,
there is a third section providing a detailed analysis and re-explanation.
This is divided into two parts.
The first part distinguishes the three matters by way of persons.
Furthermore, from the section "according to what is appropriate regarding these three points" onwards...
Distinguishing [the stages] according to the path,
there are two parts in the preceding section.
The first concerns the two vehicles.
Second, regarding the three worlds: within the former [the world of desire],
it is said that those who are attached to various desires experience the relish of craving.
Second, regarding the assembly of those who have distanced themselves from the world, one contemplates its faults and disadvantages and thereby gives rise to renunciation.
Third, regarding the assembly of those who are liberated from fetters, there is transcendence.
Next, these are categorized according to the three worlds.
Regarding the statement, "First, because of attaining mastery over desire and mastery over purity," etc.:
the Māra King is said to have attained mastery over desire because he has attained mastery within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the Brahmā King has abandoned desire and unwholesome states, he is called "Pure Sovereign.
Regarding the phrase "because they diligently cultivate the causes for that," this refers to such non-Buddhist śramaṇas and others.
Because one seeks to attain the states of Māra and Brahmā,
one cultivates the causes for those celestial realms.
Regarding the phrase "because of the various karmic causes and effects of the three realms," etc.:

Apart from the two previously mentioned [realms], all the various karmas pertaining to the destinies of gods and humans are categorized here below according to the paths among the three types of action.
First, the faults and afflictions are distinguished in relation to the two paths of seeing and cultivation;
subsequently, renunciation is distinguished in relation to the four types of liberation.
Within this context, the "taste of craving" (āsvāda) is not explained in detail.
Regarding the analysis within the section on liberation:
first is the teaching (dharma),
followed by the analogy (upamā).
Later, in the *Fashuo* (Exposition of the Dharma),
Master Tai said:
The former greed is internal;
the latter greed is external.
It is greed regarding the five objects of desire.
Therefore, it must be further clarified. Master Da said:
"The first three characteristics distinguish [the state of] nirvana with remainder."
The last of the characteristics distinguishes *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
its meaning can be understood.
Regarding the analogy:
First, five metaphors are employed to illustrate the obstacles belonging to the four types of liberation;
subsequently, four statements are presented to conclude these five metaphors.
Within the former section:
The statement, "For example, suppose there is a person who arrives at either a copper or an iron [fetter]," is the first simile;
it refers to being bound by the three poisons.
Alternatively, wood symbolizes greed;
a rope symbolizes hatred;
and iron symbolizes delusion.
Furthermore, regarding the second simile concerning the stationing of other persons to guard it:
it refers to being guarded by the latent tendencies of the three poisons and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
Alternatively, regarding those who have reached that state and intend to bring it back,
there is a third analogy:
through the mundane path, one suppresses and eliminates greed and other afflictions to give rise to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti).
Because those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as greed still grasp at the future, they cause one to remain within the lower realms; how much less could one possibly escape them?
The fourth metaphor illustrates how the power of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) prevents the practice of equanimity regarding the bonds of greed and so forth.
Or there may be those who are even unwilling to escape;
the fifth simile represents them as being bound by the nine fetters and developing attachment to pleasure within that place where they experience the five sublime sensual desires.
The following four lines summarize the preceding five metaphors.
Master Jing said:
"In this way, that person is bound by all manner of bonds."
This is the first. Regarding "that which is guarded by the guardians of skillful means," this collectively clarifies that the second,
third, and fourth [stages] constitute the second [category].
"Those bound by the most firm fetters" generally clarifies the fourth [category];
"those bound by the nine fetters" constitutes the third.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and being harmed by enemies according to their desires," this is added separately as the fourth.
If there is anyone who can be liberated from these four bonds:
This is called liberation from all bonds.
Master Da said:
"Those who are bound by what binds them..."
The section beginning with "Having used the three poisons as a metaphor as a skillful means" concludes the preceding [discussion] and exhorts one to maintain vigilance.
In this context, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not compared [to the fetters],
because they are already established as being the most inferior; rather, it is the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are compared [to them].
The section beginning with "Next, as for enemies" and so forth concludes the analogy regarding the various sufferings, such as birth.
As for the term "beating": it refers to striking.
The previous mention of the *skandha-māra* (the demon of the aggregates), or alternatively, of being dismembered, is a metaphor for the *mṛtyu-māra* (the demon of death);
or [the mention of] being struck with staffs and whips.
The metaphor of the celestial Māra (devaputra-māra) refers to this; or, the metaphor of one who completely severs life refers to the māra of afflictions (kleśa-māra).
In the commentary,
Master Jing says: "Thus,
regarding that [passage], 'up to the bondage of greed, hatred, and delusion' is a metaphor."
This corresponds to the first analogy.
Regarding the "fools of the three worlds," the three refer to Māra, Brahmā, and others.
Those who maintain the prohibitions are like those who engage in improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and have not yet uprooted their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
this corresponds to the second [case].
Because of improper reflection, they arrive and then flee far away.
The first corresponds to the fourth [section].
"The afflictions and latent tendencies have not yet been uprooted, so they seize them again and carry them back" corresponds to the third.
These three intermediate groups are combined as the second [section].
The lovely and exquisite desires are likened to the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth;
these are joined with the fifth metaphor to form three [sections].
Furthermore, following the four maras and their adversaries,
these two types are added to constitute the fourth.
If one is liberated from these four names, one is said to understand all.
The Master Da said:
"Regarding 'bound by various things' up to 'bound by greed, anger,
and delusion,' this corresponds to the first analogy of the three poisons."

The passage beginning with "those who observe the prohibitions" below corresponds to the second and third analogies for the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the phrase "lovely and wonderful sensual desires":
This illustrates the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*). The phrase "due to those fetters," and so forth,
corresponds to the fifth analogy regarding the suffering of birth and the rest.
The section beginning with "Since he has already done so" corresponds to the initial simile in the concluding text;
the section beginning with "Having employed skillful means" follows.
The second analogy within the section on application begins with "most firm" and so forth.
Regarding the third analogy within the section on application, it states: "Furthermore, there are the four demonic enemies."
This corresponds to the fourth analogy.
In the second major section, "Explaining the Concise Teaching," etc.,
eleven gates are first set forth in verse.
First, the concise teaching;
second, the fruit of the teaching;
third, cultivation.
Four are included among the defeats;
five are abandoned through the three types of thorough knowledge;
six are fetters.
7. The seven liberations;
8. The defilements of views and conceit;
9. The phrases for pure exposition.
The ten [factors] of distancing from the four [bases], and the eleven perfections;
in the prose commentary, these constitute eleven sections.
Regarding the first section on the "Brief Teaching," concerning the request for a brief instruction based on three causes and conditions,
Master Jing says:
First, merely hearing the Dharma briefly is sufficient to achieve one's own purpose;
second, because there is fear regarding the gateways to be entered, one employs many skillful means to enter them, thinking, "May it not cause my attention to become distracted," and so forth.
Third, regarding all these dharmas thus heard and reflected upon, one cannot determine which among them one should rely upon.
For these three reasons, he briefly requested instruction.
There is an explanation:

first, for those who believe that merely hearing [the teachings] constitutes the ultimate goal, the Great Master speaks to them to produce such an understanding, thinking: "Merely hearing the Dharma in brief is sufficient to attain one's own purpose; what need is there for extensive learning and so forth?"
Why is this? Because right practice is the reality, whereas the desire for extensive learning is abandoned.
Second, because there is fear regarding the numerous contemplative practices to be performed within the dharma-gates entered.
Because the Great Master employs skillful means to enable one to enter [the path],
thirdly, by means of properly hearing and reflecting upon many teachings, he prevents the mind from becoming distracted.
Furthermore, regarding what has been heard and reflected upon as described above:
This concludes the general explanation of requesting instruction.
Second, regarding the resolution of the fruit of the teaching,
Master Jing says:
This refers to going forth for this purpose and going forth in this manner.
First, regarding the physical appearance:
shaving the hair and donning dyed robes.
First, because his form is identical to the body of the unsurpassed Buddhas;
second, as for the fulfillment of activities,
he attains the activities of the three trainings in the present life.
Third, the perfection of intention is the attainment of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) spontaneously.
Fourth, the perfection of the basis for relinquishing and acquiring is as follows:
Because one relies on internal realization, one abandons saṃsāra and takes up nirvāṇa;
it is also possible to abandon precepts and take up liberation, and so forth.
It is said that by relying fully upon this, one attains unsurpassed [enlightenment].
As explained above, Tai said:
"One leaves the household life for the sake of attaining this unsurpassed path."
And as for these three subsequent types of renunciation: what are the four?
First, by relying on this, one attains the unsurpassed attainment.
This refers to being endowed with the perfection of physical form.

Second is "attainment in the present life," which refers to the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in the present life that can give rise to the activities of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The third [type] attains it spontaneously.
Because they possess the resolute intention (*āśaya*) that arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the roots of virtue such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*),
they enter the path of seeing spontaneously.
Fourth is internal realization (*pratyātmādhigama*).

Because one abandons the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and fully assumes that of a noble one (*ārya*) upon entering the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one internally realizes the true reality (*tattva*).
There is an interpretation that [one] goes forth for the sake of this True Dharma, and goes forth in accordance with the True Dharma.
Now, examining the text, it states:
"The discourse on the Sūtra says, 'Possessing [the precepts], one relies upon this to attain supreme [enlightenment],' and so forth."
This complete phrase should belong to the preceding sentence.
Why does it belong to the following?
One must not rely exclusively [on this].
The third explanation is concluded.
It states that there are six kinds of death;
the first two are easily understood.

Death through lack of self-discipline refers to one who, having failed to discipline their conduct and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) in past lives, likewise fails to discipline their body and underlying tendencies in this present life, and dies; having died, they give rise to a future personal existence.
Furthermore, regarding the inclusion of those who possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and whose conduct leads them to be bound by various sufferings and fettered by craving and so forth:
"those who die having been tamed" refers to those who pass away after having already subdued their latent dispositions in the present life.
The future self-entity will no longer arise. Regarding those who die with their homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*):
this refers to those who, like those in the past whose underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) were unsubdued, likewise fail to subdue them in the present and then relinquish their physical life.
Regarding those such as Yashasvin and Mṛta:
if one was undisciplined in the past but has already attained discipline at the time of death in the present, [one is called disciplined].
This is called death in a dissimilar state (*asabhāga-maraṇa*).
As for the statement "if, in the present, [there are] even those formations belonging to a similar state (*sabhāga*)," it should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, from this point downward, there are two aspects of death:
namely, the characteristics of the faults of saṃsāra and the benefits of its cessation.
Below, these two will be explained.
The meaning is clear and can be understood.
Regarding the fourth [point], the explanation of falling into numerical categories is as previously analyzed.
Fifth, regarding the explanation that through three characteristics one should understand the thorough knowledge and abandonment of non-self:
first, thoroughly knowing non-self within;
second, thoroughly knowing the absence of "mine" without.
Third, regarding both the internal and external, there is nothing further that is mutually bound;
by practicing this, one abandons those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and attains their ultimate cessation.
This is the sixth [section], explaining the three kinds of bonds.
Regarding the statement "it is called 'various' because it arises initially from various [causes]":
the eight fetters are not one;
therefore, they are called "various."
Regarding the statement that, among these, while there is only one kind of conditioned object, there are five kinds of conditioned objects of perception:
since the conception of a self as non-existent is identical to the characteristic of non-existence itself, it need not be established separately from the [other] factors.
If one calculates that there must be distinct dharmas of existence, there are five types.
In the seventh explanation, regarding liberation,
there are briefly two kinds of thorough knowledge of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
First, one realizes the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*) by means of the four modes of practice, such as determination through impermanence;
second, one realizes the nature of things in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) by means of the eleven modes, such as the past and so forth.
In the eighth section, the "Explanation of Pride through Views," first pride based on views is elucidated;
subsequently, the establishment of the four types of persons regarding the abandonment of defilements is presented.
It should be understood that among the former, there are two types that ought to be abandoned:
namely, views and pride.
These views and pride are differentiated into five categories.
By way of two doors— namely,
by way of manifestation (*paryavasthāna*), by way of bondage (*bandhana*), and by way of latent tendency (*anuśaya*)—
it becomes threefold through manifestation.
That is to say, this "I," "mine," and "I-conceit" are established as one [hindrance] by virtue of being an envelopment;
that is, attachment.
That is to say, the prior notions of "I" and "mine," as well as pride, when they manifest and give rise to attachment, are called "envelopments" (paryavasthāna);
the seeds of these three are called "latent tendencies" (anuśaya).
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, there is the body of consciousness up to the causal characteristics of latent tendencies":
It clarifies that the conscious body and external phenomena serve as the causal characteristics for the preceding five types.
This sentence is the general statement;
from here on, it is explained in detail.

Regarding the statement that "these causal characteristics (*nimitta*) are twofold," up to the point where the conception of a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) take the conscious body as their objective causal characteristic:
this self and the conceit of self take one's own five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—the conscious body—as their objective characteristic (*ālambana-nimitta*).
In the second principle, consciousness is taken as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) aspect;
this is omitted and not explained.
As for the reckoning of what I have established as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) aspect, it consists of two kinds.

Taken collectively, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) as well as external mountains, rivers, and so forth, constitute the objective aspect (*ālambananimitta*) of what belongs to the self.
Furthermore, one should also regard the existence of the aggregate of consciousness as the causal condition (*pratyayanimitta*);
however, this is also omitted and not explicitly stated.

Because within the collection of consciousnesses there exist the seeds of the notions of "I," "mine," and "I-am-ness," that attachment takes the hearing of incorrect teachings and so forth as its causes, conditions, and causal characteristics.
The fourth attachment takes false hearing,
false causes and conditions, and false teachings as its causal characteristic,
and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) as its causal characteristic.
Regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) acting as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to their characteristic of being a cause:

among the five [types of causes] mentioned previously, the fifth latent disposition acts as the causal condition by means of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that manifest erroneously (*ayathābhūta*), which are able to perfume [the mind].
Because it cannot take an object as its condition, there is no causal characteristic of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Below, the establishment of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) is presented in relation to four types of persons;
this affliction is precisely the five factors mentioned previously.
This refers to the obsessions (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the notions of "I" and "mine" and the conceit of "I am.
To say that while these factors exist in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their grasping cannot be found,
means that an ordinary person who has entered the Dharma remains within the seven stages of preparation (*saptaprayoga*) and has suppressed such grasping.
There are four kinds [of causes] as well as the cause for the conscious body (*vijñānakāya*).
Furthermore, there is a portion of the characteristics of the cause for attachment, namely, the conscious body itself;
it is not merely the aforementioned four kinds of causes.
This is also a characteristic cause for partial attachment.
Regarding the statement that "among those in training, [the self] is entirely unfindable":
the practitioner in training has already abandoned the conceptualized views of "self" and "mine" that are to be abandoned through insight.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the cause for that conscious body,
one also abandons the third attachment and the fourth underlying tendency (*anuśaya*).
As for the statement "and the attachment to the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna) along with its causal characteristics":
One is able to sever all views, the conceit of self (asmimāna), attachments, and their causal characteristics; yet,
it is said that the latent tendency (anuśaya) of the conceit of self can still be found.
Because one has abandoned the conceptualization of a self,
the cultivation of abandonment prevents the manifestation of the conceit "I am";
nevertheless, the latent tendency (anuśaya) of the conceit "I am" can still be found.
Furthermore, regarding all the practices of non-Buddhist sentient beings that do not serve to sever those [afflictions],
they apply mental attention toward the abandonment of desire among the four types of clinging (*upādāna*),
while practicing in accordance with their own views within the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*).
One abandons those actions performed toward others that do not accord with one's own inclinations.
As for the grasping at a self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*), all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not say it is abandoned;
they claim, "This dharma is distinct from the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and even applies to those who further practice correctly."
That which obstructs the path of seeing is called "having severed one part," while that which obstructs the path of cultivation is called "severing the remaining parts.
Ninth, there are eight phrases explaining the statement on purity.
First, regarding the statement "because one transcends views and conceit, it is called the two kinds, etc.":
the combination of the two—self (*ātman*) and what belongs to self (*ātmīya*)—is termed "view" and "conceit based on view.

Second, regarding the statement "because one eliminates their causal characteristics, it is called the phrase 'purity through the removal of characteristics'": [this refers to the elimination of the causes of those views and conceits].
Excluding the causal characteristics of the conscious body:
third, by severing attachment;
fourth, by severing the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The fifth refers to one who, regarding future existence, has already severed craving and attachment;
because they no longer perform actions that lead to future existence,
this is called "severing craving and attachment."
Regarding "the sixth and the transformation of the three fetters":
it is called "transformation" because of the abandonment of the three fetters.
Regarding "the seventh, namely, the clear realization of correct pride": [it refers to the pride that arises from having attained such realization].
Master Jing said:
"In the original manuscript, it still says 'zhengzi' (rectifier of characters).
The Tripiṭaka Master said it should read 'zhiman' (ceasing arrogance)."
Because the conceit of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has been exhausted, it is called "the cessation of conceit" (*mānasthiti*).
The Tripiṭaka Master further stated:
"However, it may also be understood as 'correct understanding' (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)."
This refers to an adept (aśaikṣa) who forms the understanding of the four noble truths— such as "my births are exhausted"—
while still maintaining the notion of a self; this is called pride (*māna*),
yet it is not false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
Therefore, it is called "right pride" (*samyag-māna*).
Master Tai said: "Because it is the pride [arising from] correct direct realization (*samyak-abhisamaya*)."
Another interpretation is that it should be stated as "the clear realization that halts views and pride.
The treatise refers to this in terms of the primary obstacles.
Therefore, it is said that only "right pride" (*sammā-māna*) is taught.
Master Dada also stated:
"The Tripiṭaka contains two interpretations."
One version states that this character "zhèng" (正) is an error and should be "zhǐ" (止).
One who has attained the state beyond training never again gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Therefore, it is said that they "cease arrogance.
Among them, although practitioners do not intentionally give rise to arrogance,
they do give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Furthermore, it is said that the term "right" (samyak) is not incorrect;
even those beyond training (aśaikṣa) give rise to [the thought] "my births are ended," and so forth,
and they should likewise give rise to right conceit (samyag-māna).
Because they are spoken of as "pride" by way of designation.
As for the eighth, "having already brought an end to suffering," all such [factors] are collectively subsumed into one;
these eight are collectively termed the single "phrase of pure teaching."
Tenth, the explanation of the four types of separation:
first, "dwelling without a second" means abandoning the Buddha.
Regarding "reclining furniture at the limit of the two locations," Master Jing says it refers to dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
Master Tai said:
"The term 'limit' (bianji) has two meanings.
First, using the lower parts of things such as weeds as bedding."
Second, being at the furthest limit in accordance with the Dharma;
third, physical seclusion that can be known;
fourth, mental seclusion.
Within this, there are three successive explanations:
first, the abandonment of unwholesome discursive thoughts;
second, the arousal of diligent effort through five aspects.
The third [section] concerns the abandonment of the hindrances to śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The eleventh [section] explains the three perfections;
the meaning of the textual passages is clear.
